title: Diving into Kronecker Adapters: Component Design Matters
claim: Without a scaling factor, gradient norms differ widely across component configurations; with a configuration-aware scaling, they align to the same scale.
layout: 2 vertically stacked line plots, top-to-bottom, shared axes, math captions beneath each
description: Two vertically stacked line charts, both plotting gradient norm on the y-axis against training steps (0 to 25) on the x-axis. Each chart shows five colored curves (purple, red, green, orange, yellow) for different component configurations. Panel (a), labeled λ≡1, shows the curves widely separated. Purple sits near 1.0, red near 0.35, green near 0.25, orange near 0.2, and yellow near 0.05, so the gradient norms differ by an order of magnitude. Panel (b), labeled λ = 16/√(r·r2), shows all curves collapsed into a tight band between roughly 0.6 and 0.8. They share the same jagged up-and-down pattern and only diverge slightly after step 15. Math captions sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the spread in the top panel, then to the convergence in the bottom one.
caption: Gradient norm during training with (a) $\lambda \equiv1$ and (b) $\lambda = \frac{16}{\sqrt{r\cdot r_2}}$ under different $r_1$, $r_2$ and $r$. Identical colors indicate identical component configurations. Our method maintains gradient norms at the same scale across different component configurations.
abstract: Kronecker adapters have emerged as a promising approach for fine-tuning large-scale models, enabling high-rank updates through tunable component structures. However, existing work largely treats the component structure as a fixed or heuristic design choice, leaving the dimensions and number of Kronecker components underexplored. In this paper, we identify component structure as a key factor governing the capacity of Kronecker adapters. We perform a fine-grained analysis of both the dimensions and number of Kronecker components. In particular, we show that the alignment between Kronecker adapters and full fine-tuning depends on component configurations. Guided by these insights, we propose Component Designed Kronecker Adapters (CDKA). We further provide parameter-budget-aware configuration guidelines and a tailored training stabilization strategy for practical deployment. Experiments across various architectures and modalities demonstrate the effectiveness of CDKA. Code is available at https://github.com/rainstonee/CDKA.
